units.text: A qualitative assessment of barriers within the university learning environment and their influence on students' participation in engineering education
Background

Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) play a crucial role in socioeconomic development and in combating poverty and other development challenges.Engineers help shape the world, contribute to economic growth, enhance the quality of life, and tackle global issues by designing infrastructure, developing technologies, and solving complex challenges in energy, transportation, healthcare, and sustainability (UNESCO, 2021).Nations such as Japan and Germany that prioritised engineering have reaped substantial benefits but the same cannot be said for Africa with less than 5% of the world's engineers (Mohammed, 2023).Addressing societal problems through the application of STEM requires an adequate number and quality of expertise including men and women.However, challenges of STEM human resource development have thwarted the efforts of Africa to reap the benefits of STEM (OECD, 2007).

Though fewer engineers are present in Africa compared to some advanced countries, the number is largely skewed towards men, and this has been attributed to several factors including the observation by UNESCO (2017) that girls globally tend to lose interest in STEM subjects as they age.This decrease in interest is reflected in their participation rates at higher educational levels-women make up only 35% of all students enrolled in STEMrelated fields.Within the female student population in higher education worldwide, only about 30% choose to study STEM disciplines, and variations exist among different fields (UNESCO, 2017).Specifically, female enrolment is notably low in the following areas: Information and Communication Technology (3%); natural sciences, mathematics, and statistics (5%); engineering, manufacturing, and construction (8%); and health and welfare studies (15%).The gender gap in participation and achievement in STEM education has been extensively researched over many years (Becker, 1989;Hyde et al., 1990).Although gender differences in science and mathematics achievement have shown signs of improvement in many countries, as indicated by large-scale cross-national surveys (Mullis et al., 2016), these differences have not been eliminated (Mullis et al., 2016;OECD, 2016).

Because women constitute about 49.71% of the world's population (World Bank, 2023), their contributions to the labour market in all fields cannot be ignored as men alone cannot meet the labour requirements for engineering and other fields.However, in many developed and developing countries, women's participation in engineering is low.In Ghana, there is currently no national statistics on men and women's enrolment in engineering, however at institutional levels, some statistics can be obtained.For example, at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), which is the foremost university that started offering engineering since its establishment in 1952, female enrolment in engineering has increased over an 18-year period-from 12.2% in the 2003/2004 academic year to 18.1% in 2020/2021 academic year (Omari & Kouevi, 2023).Even within the 18 engineering programmes offered at KNUST, gender disparity exists where, for example, female enrolment in 2020/21 academic year was highest in Biomedical engineering (40.1%) followed by Petrochemical engineering (27.2%),Chemical engineering (25.8%),Computer engineering (11.6%) with Automobile engineering being the least with 3.7% female population.The University of Ghana, the oldest in the country, established the School of Engineering Sciences in 2003/2004 academic year and currently runs five programmes (i.e.Agricultural Engineering, Biomedical Engineering, Computer Engineering, Food Process Engineering, and Materials Science Engineering-Ceramics Option).Its first cohort of students consisted of five females and 26 males.The University of Mines and Technology is another public university in Ghana that runs engineering programmes.It was previously a faculty affiliated to KNUST College of Engineering but became an autonomous university in 2004.In 2012/2013 academic year, female undergraduate enrolment in engineering was 15% and it increased to 25% in 2013/2014 academic year (Kilu & Sanda, 2016).Some Polytechnics and Technical Universities in Ghana also run engineering programmes leading to the award of various certificates such as diploma, higher national diploma (HND) and Bachelor of Technology (BTech).

Several reasons have been ascribed to explain the low rates of students participation in STEM education and careers.For women in particular, these include social and environmental factors such as stereotypes, cultural beliefs, lack of self-confidence, implicit bias, and systemic barriers such as theoretical, unfriendly and genderinsensitive teaching methodologies (Mansfield et al., 2014;UNESCO, 2017).Other researchers categorised the barriers to low students' participation in STEM into individual; family and peer; school; and societal level factors (Kolmos et al., 2013;McDaniel, 2015;Spearman & Watt, 2013).School-level barriers include negative learning environments such as career advisers' lack of support for potential engineering students, and masculine biases in engineering curriculum and assessment methods, which do not favour females in particular (Godfrey & King, 2011).

Efforts are being made all over the world to encourage more students especially women to study engineering however, some students leave engineering majors prior to graduation (Geisinger & Raman, 2013).In the USA, about half of those pursuing an engineering major change their field of study or drop out before graduation, and half do so during their first year of college (Flanigan, 2024).A review of literature by Geisinger and Raman (2013) on issues related to student attrition and retention in the field of engineering revealed that the low retention rate could be the result of engineering programmes often involving very traditional types of teaching.These include students facing difficulties in understanding course material; students feeling discouraged due to competitive grading structures; lack of self-efficacy or self-confidence; inadequate high school preparation; failure of engineering and course material to capture student interest; and other obstacles due to gender, race, or ethnicity.A systematic review by Kayan-Fadlelmula et al. (2022) revealed that environmental factors such as family and parental influence, stereotypes, and biases are barriers affecting student retention in STEM.Other studies such as Talley and Martinez Ortiz (2017) and Dost (2024) examined factors that contribute to the interest development and motivational drive for women's retention in STEM.

In Ghana, factors within the learning environments that influence students' participation and retention in engineering education are not well understood hence the objective of this paper was to qualitatively explore and examine the barriers within the learning environment and how they influence students' participation in engineering education at the university level.To achieve the objective, the following research questions were answered:
(1) What challenges do engineering students face within the learning environment that could serve as barriers to their effective participation and retention in engineering education?

(2) How do these barriers affect the experiences of female and male students?Answering these questions provided insights into the factors that could contribute to the low students' participation, retention and performance in engineering education, and how they affect women and men differently.The study also provided some pointers for reducing the barriers and enhancing students' experiences in the engineering learning environment.
Theoretical background

This section illuminates how the interaction of gender stereotypes and learning environments contributes to gender disparities in engineering education.It enhances our understanding of the theoretical underpinnings of gender disparities in learning environments and provides a foundation for designing interventions that address these challenges.Thus, the concept of the learning environment, feminist pedagogy theory and expectation states theory as well as their combined effects on students learning experiences are discussed in the next paragraphs.
The concept of learning environments

Learning environments, which constitute the physical, pedagogical, and social and psychological contexts in which teaching and learning take place, have been found useful in influencing students learning experiences (Closs et al., 2022;Rusticus et al., 2023;UNESCO, 2012).Good learning environments are associated with increased students' interest in their field of study, enhanced students' performances, better understanding of career paths and reduced chances of dropouts (Rusticus et al., 2023).Learning environments however differ based on contexts.Closs et al. (2022) proposed three dimensions of a learning environment -the physical, pedagogical, and psychosocial.The physical dimension of a learning environment comprises the physical structure including furniture (Hannafin & Land, 1997) and can inspire or inhibit different teaching strategies (Beckers, 2019).Baars et al. (2020) define a physical learning environment (PLE) as a school-built environment that is intended as a learning place.It includes school buildings and learning spaces and their spatial structure, furniture, fittings and equipment.Barrett et al. (2015) organised various aspects of PLE into subdimensions of naturalness, individualisation and stimulation, where (i) naturalness refers to environmental aspects affecting physical comfort and well-being, including the climate conditions, sound and light; (ii) individualisation refers to the functional aspects supporting the learning and teaching activities of students and teachers, including the flexibility of the PLE, the connection between spaces, and users' control over use and design of the PLE; and (iii) stimulation refers to the aesthetic aspects stimulating learning behaviour, including the complexity of the PLE and the use of colours.

The pedagogical dimension of the learning environment entails the activities, methods and strategies involved in facilitating students' learning (Hannafin & Land, 1997;Skordi & Fraser, 2019).It includes the combination of teaching methods (what instructors do), learning activities (what instructors ask their students to do), and learning assessments (the assignments, projects, or tasks that measure students' learning).The psychosocial dimension (PSLE) refers to all psychological and social factors involved in the learning process (Cleveland & Fisher, 2014).It relates to human behaviour including student cohesiveness, equity and teacher support (Dorman, 2014;Skordi & Fraser, 2019).Moos (1980) identifies three subdimensions of the psychosocial learning environment (PSLE), namely, personal development, relationships, and system maintenance and change.Based on Moos (1980), personal development refers to the directions of personal growth and self-enhancement, including students' autonomy and affinity with the learning content.Relationships refer to the nature and intensity of personal relationships within the learning environment; the involvement of people; and feelings of being affiliated, accepted and supported.System maintenance and change refers to order, control, expectations and responsiveness to change, including grouping of students and teachers' scheduling and regulation of the learning process.The psychosocial aspect of the learning environment depicts how relationships with a friend, peer or lecturer can hinder or foster the motivation to learn and have a deep impact on student outcomes (Chamliss & Takacs, 2014).

In line with the dimensions of learning environments, Rusticus et al. (2023) report that the key considerations for increasing students' interest in their field of studies and reducing dropout rates include active engagement of students in class, provision of supporting materials, approachability of faculty, and creation of a safe space for students to ask or answer questions without the fear of being judged.The other considerations Rusticus et al. (2023) suggested were class structure, infrastructure, and institutional setting such as class size, classroom design and residence on campus.A critical aspect of the learning environment which is often overlooked is the role of gender and ethnicity.A male-dominated learning and practical sessions and the absence of girls-specific facilities could demotivate female students and restrict their active participation (Closs et al., 2022;UNESCO, 2012).These show how complex the learning environment isit is not only about the physical, pedagogical and psychosocial dimensions, but also the interaction of several factors depending on the contexts.By acknowledging and addressing power dynamics, stereotypes, and issues related to learning environments, it is possible to design more equitable and inclusive engineering educational experiences, ultimately working towards gender parity in this critical field.This study offers a roadmap for future research and interventions aimed at dismantling the barriers that hinder students' progress in engineering education.
Feminist pedagogy

Critical feminist pedagogy, inspired by Freire (1970) and developed by scholars such as Hooks (1994) focuses on the creation of inclusive and empowering learning environments that challenge traditional power structures and promote social justice.It refers to a fusion of critical and feminist pedagogies that enables girls and boys to develop a feminist consciousness by raising their critical awareness of oppressive social norms, power structures, traditions, and the gender relations that impact them (Freire et al., 2014).Relevant to this study is the feminist pedagogy which prioritises power and empowerment; identities and intersectionality; and knowledge and personal experience as important considerations in classroom dynamics and learning environments (Bostow et al., 2015).In the context of engineering education, it sheds light on how teaching methods, curriculum design, and classroom dynamics can perpetuate or challenge gender disparities.The feminist pedagogy illustrates the interplay between pedagogical and psychosocial learning environments such that within the context of higher engineering education, this theory offers strategies to deconstruct traditional, male-centric engineering curricula (Smith, 2016) and introduce diverse perspectives and voices to reflect a broader range of experiences.It also fosters inclusive teaching methods that prioritise collaboration, critical thinking, and active learning (Borrego et al., 2010) and creates classroom environments where diverse voices are heard, valued, and actively included, addressing discrimination and microaggressions (Bensimonet al., 2004).The feminist pedagogy further shows how the shortfalls in the physical learning environment such as overcrowded classrooms and lack of learning facilities can influence the pedagogical environments and subsequently the psychosocial or emotional experiences of students.This is supported by Rusticus et al. (2023), Closs et al. (2022), Beckers (2019) and UNESCO (2012) who report that large class sizes affect teaching strategies, reduce active participation of students in class as well as their ability to express themselves more freely.
Expectation states theory

The Expectation States Theory (Berger et al., 1974) posits that people evaluate others' competence based on specific skills and abilities relevant to the task at hand, and status characteristics including gender, age, physique, or race that can lead people to believe someone will be successful, even if those characteristics are irrelevant to the task.Gender roles are formed in early childhood and continue to influence behaviour through adolescence and adulthood, including the choice of academic majors and careers.In many countries, men are underrepresented in communal roles in health care, elementary education, and domestic functions, that is, the HEED fields (Croft et al., 2015) whereas women are underrepresented in the STEM fields (Beede et al., 2011) and top leadership positions (Leopold et al., 2016).This gender role expectations can thus shape the allocation of jobs, tasks, and responsibilities even in learning environments.The expectation states theory suggests that gender role expectations cause perceivers to display supportive or more critical behaviour towards a person, depending on the extent to which that the person is believed to hold task-relevant knowledge and abilities.The more these gender role expectations suggest that a target person has the knowledge and abilities for a task (e.g.men on male-typed tasks), the more the perceiver will support the person by granting the person opportunities to act, evaluating the person more positively (Correll & Ridgeway, 2003;Wittenbaum & Bowman, 2005).Conversely, if gender role expectations suggest that a person does not hold task-relevant knowledge and abilities (e.g.female on male-typed tasks), such a person tends to be victim of various unsupportive behaviours of perceivers including ignoring or interrupting the person, evaluating her or him more negatively or discrediting the person (Foschi, 2000).In turn, such unsupportive behaviours make it more likely that women and men in gender role-incongruent roles fail or quit.

In educational settings, expectation states theory can help provide insights into how teachers' and peers' expectations about students' abilities, based on perceived status characteristics such as age, gender, race and physique, can influence tasks allocations as well as their interactions and outcomes.Expectation states theory can help educators and policymakers to create more equitable learning environments by addressing biases and promoting inclusive practices.
Methodology
Development of an interview guide

This is an exploratory study, hence, focus group discussions were conducted with undergraduate university students enrolled in engineering programmes at a public Ghanaian university.The aim was to identify and understand their experiences as they interact with their mates, lecturers and other staff and how these interactions could serve as barriers to their effective participation and retention in engineering programmes.As noted by Basch (1987), group interviews are a valuable tool for gaining insights into how people think and learn about their personal life situations.To help guide the discussion, an interview guide was prepared by the research team.The discussion questions can be found in the publication by Omari and Kouevi (2023).The questions were largely informed by published works such as Hill et al. (2010) who examined why there are few women in STEM as published by the American Association of University Women (AAUW).The interview guide also benefited from the report published by UNESCO (2012) that presents a comprehensive review of research on learning environments from multiple perspectives including those that focused on the physical and psychosocial environment and organisational climate of classrooms.The experiences of some of the researchers who had their education in STEM fields also helped in formulating some of the questions.The discussions broadly focused on barriers and challenges within the university system, as well as barriers related to societal and cultural factors, including misconceptions that could affect students' participation and retention in engineering programmes once they have been enrolled.Some of the discussion questions were:

• What do you find most challenging as an engineering student?How have you coped with the challenges?• Why do you think there are fewer/more women in your engineering class?In your opinion, do you think women/men are intimidated in class because of their low numbers?• Are there any noticeable differences when you are taught by a man or a woman?• Do you think the teaching facilities and methods of teaching (theory and practical) influence your understanding of some courses?What is wrong with the teaching methods and the facilities?What do you think can be done to improve the teaching methods?• Have you ever experienced a situation where women were not involved in some tasks in your class?What were these tasks?How did you feel about that?• Do you sometimes feel intimidated by the opposite sex during academic work including practical sessions?• Does the opposite sex prevent or discourage you from performing certain tasks, especially during practical sessions?• Do you sometimes feel that the opposite sex can perform certain tasks better than you?

What are these tasks?• Which aspect of engineering do you find unexciting?Does that make you regret being an engineering student?• Are you aware of any of students who have stopped offering engineering or changed their programmes from engineering to other programmes?If yes, what were the reasons?
• Have you ever contemplated stopping or changing your engineering programme?
Recruitment of focus group participants

The focus group discussions (FGDs) were held with engineering students during the COVID-19 pandemic when schools were closed hence, the Executives of the Engineering Students Association of a Ghanaian university were contacted to mobilise the students residing in and around Accra for the discussions held physically at the researchers' workplace.In total, six focus groups were held (one each for females and males in the second, third and fourth years of their studies).First year students were not involved in the study because their admission into the university was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic.Both female and male students were recruited for the focus group discussions to enable us to identify issues peculiar to each sex as well as those common to both sexes.The involvement of both females and males also allowed us to verify with the opposite sex some of the issues that came out of the interviews.It also allowed us to get a better understanding of how each sex views and interacts with the other.To validate the data during the interviews, references were made to several issues raised by participants in the previous interviews to seek their views and confirmations.

For example, we asked the male students 'your female counterparts said you (the males) do not allow them to take part in practical tasks, is that true?' The responses provided helped us to validate what has been said previously.

Though the selection of the FGD participants was largely based on the willingness of students to participate, the Executives ensured that almost all the engineering programmes were represented.One focus group was held per day in the month of November 2020 with each lasting between one and half and two hours.Table 1 shows the number of male and female students per focus group.The same interview guide was used in all the six focus groups, enabling the research team to reach a saturation point where no new information was generated, and findings became repetitive.Thus, the data represented the general opinions, perceptions and experiences of engineering students at the public university we studied.

All FGDs were recorded and later transcribed verbatim.Content analysis of the transcripts was conducted using Atlas.tisoftware to identify themes and categories related to common and gendered barriers to students' participation in engineering education.The coding was done by one researcher using a deductive approach largely informed by the three dimensions of the learning environment followed by the identification of common themes under each dimension.The findings from the FGDs were discussed with selected engineering lecturers in the studied university, at an information-gathering workshop because some of the issues raised by the students concerned them and so their views were needed.The lecturers confirmed most of the issues expressed by the students and provided recommendations for improving the learning environment and students' learning experiences and outcomes.
Findings

The major barriers confronting engineering students within learning environments have been categorised into three main areas.Firstly, barriers within the physical learning environment, which include inadequate or overcrowded lecture rooms and insufficient laboratory space and equipment.Secondly, barriers within the pedagogical learning environment encompassing inadequate practical sessions, outmoded curriculum, poor teaching methods, and a lack of orientation for students about the engineering programme and what to expect during their studies.Thirdly, barriers related to the psychosocial environment, which include limited female involvement in practical work, backlash and apathetic attitudes when women assume leadership roles in group activities, the intimidation and silencing of female students in class, and a scarcity of female role models.These barriers are discussed in detail in the subsequent paragraphs, with supporting evidence, including quotes from both female and male students.Appendices 1 and 2 show the number of participants whose quotes were included in the texts based on sex, engineering programme and level of study.
Barriers within the physical learning environment
Inadequate chairs and overcrowded lecture rooms

In terms of inadequate chairs and overcrowded lecture rooms, both female and male students complained that the chairs were not enough, so some students rush to occupy the front seats.Moreover, the lecturers do not speak loud enough for those at the back to hear since there were no properly functioning microphones, and that affects their understanding of lessons.In the first year especially when many students take common courses, some of the classes are large and some of the students are not used to such large numbers.These were the concerns of several students in the following quotes: The overcrowded lecture rooms do not only affect the students, but lecturers as well as expressed by a third-year female Civil Engineering student (3FE3) and a fourth-year female Electrical Engineering student (4FE9) in the following quotes:
"When I

"We usually have two classes with the biomedical engineering students, so the lecture room gets so fully packed.Apart from students not hearing most of the lecture, even the lecturer has a restricted space to move around while lecturing" [third-year female Civil Eng.3FE3]."There was a time that we got two microphones; one was placed in the middle of the auditorium and the other at the front.But event with that, you could hardly hear the lecturer.When you raise a concern that you cannot hear he would say 'I am trying'.In a way, I understood him because he looked over 60 years, and you could see that the class was too large for him to handle.God being so good, we managed" [fourthyear female Electrical Eng.4FE9].

In addition to the inadequate classroom spaces, some students, especially those residing outside campus, raised concern about lack of spaces for their private studies.Here is a quote by a second-year male Electrical Engineering student:

"For those staying off campus, we do not really have a proper place to study or hang around till the next lecture.Though the Engineering Tent was constructed with benches to allow students to sit and relax or learn, the environment is too open and noisy and thus unconducive for learning.We sometimes have to walk a long distance to the library to study" [second-year male Electrical Eng.2ME7].

When these concerns were discussed with the lecturers who participated in the information-gathering workshop, they agreed that the number of students admitted keeps increasing year after year while most of the facilities remain the same.They, however, indicated that the situation could be better managed but for some students who stubbornly stand at the back making noise.They also suggested that while the expansion of lecture rooms and recruitment of more lecturers could be helpful in the medium to long-term, the introduction of online teaching could help reduce the problem of overcrowding in the short term.
Inadequate laboratory space and equipment

The unavailability of an adequate number of functioning laboratory equipment also contributed to the challenges the students expressed about practical and fieldwork.Access to resources for scientific experiments has been associated with girls' achievement in science and interest in science subjects (Simpkins et al., 2015).According to a second-year male Computer Engineering student (2ME9), they have just a few computers working and whenever they have a certain class, the lecturer does not allow them to partake in class because he has a perception that when they use their laptops in class, they would not pay attention to him.He added:

"The software on the university's laptops is version 2004 but you are not allowed to use your own laptop that has the latest version.The lecturer however teaches us with the 2015 version, but three to five people gather around one computer and if you don't go early, you won't get space to sit, and even when you do, you can't hear what the lecturer is teaching because you are sitting at the back and there is no public address system.You must find time later and go for the videos on You-Tube.The lecturer would tell you to bring your pen drive for the software but not everyone has a laptop to pursue that course, and that is a major problem that we are facing" [second year male Computer Eng. 2ME9].

In addition to the limited and malfunctioning equipment, the laboratories are also overcrowded like the lecture rooms making the practical work ineffective.Below are quotes by two female and one male students: "In my department, the instruments are limited.In every second semester, students do field work and if you don't go early to book an instrument, you won't get a properly functioning one and that means you will not be able to do proper work and achieve the expected results" [fourth-year female Geomatic Eng.4FE8]."There are more spoilt computers than the well-functioning ones.So, three or more people gather around one computer, and it does not make learning effective.Moreover, the projectors are quite old so even when you tell the lecturer to brighten it a bit, it remains the same" [second-year male Mechanical Engineering 2ME4]."In my class, because the class size is big, we are in bigger groups.So, practical sessions are ineffective.When the groups are big, we crowd around the lab technician so you may not see well, and you may end up being confused" [second year female Electrical Eng.2FE9].
It was also realised that the high cost of some equipment and the quest to protect them from being damaged limited their usage by students.Two female students expressed this as shown below:

"In my department, they often tell us that the instruments are very expensive, so just a few are available.Because of this, when we go to the field, only a few students will have their turn to use the equipment before it is time for the next class.The lecturers encourage us to do internships so we can have more practical experience" [fourthyear female Geomatic Eng.4FE7]."We were not being allowed to use some equipment during practical.But when I did my internship in my department, I was surprised to see all those equipment in the lab and I used them with my supervisor.I was wondering why we weren't allowed to use them during practical when school is in session.Maybe they think students will damage the equipment" [fourth year female Metallurgical Eng.4FE11].
Barriers within the pedagogical learning environment
Outmoded curriculum and poor teaching methods

The concerns about outmoded curriculum and poor teaching methods were mentioned by the students as one of the challenges that could result in students losing interest in engineering.Some of the students felt that technology is advancing very fast and hence there is a need for the curriculum to be revised to suit modern trends."One time, we were to go to the automobile engineering lab to do assembling and disassembling.I was excited when we were told about it initially, so I equipped myself before the lab by watching YouTube videos on that.I was however very disappointed when we got to the lab and were just opening the top of an old engine and closing it.I didn't enjoy the practical at all" [second-year male Mechanical Eng.2ME4].
Inadequate practical sessions

The low number of practical sessions was mentioned by a female Petrochemical Engineering student (2FE3) who states that she feels she is not doing engineering because she did not expect engineering to be full of more theory than practical.The following statements also showed how three female students expressed their dissatisfaction with the low level of practical sessions compared to theoretical classes.It's like using this calculation to control this part of the machine and so on but it's as if we're still doing the pure science.We are not seeing the practical aspect of the engineering" [second-year female Electrical Eng.2FE9].

It was also revealed that the limited number of practical sessions is linked to the limited laboratory facilities.The quote below expresses these concerns about the limited laboratory space and equipment and how it affects students' participation in practical work: "The facilities are not enough compared to the number of students.I thought as engineering students we should be having practical about five times a week.But in the first semester of my first year, we spent considerable amount of time in theory classes than going to the labs.Even anytime there is a scheduled lab, they will tell us that the third years and fourth years were having practical so we cannot have access to the lab.I think this happens this way because the facilities are not enough for the students.I guess that limited facilities is a major reason for scheduling more theory classes than practical" [second year male Civil engineering 2ME6].

A fourth-year female Agricultural Engineering student (4FE6) however said that they have been doing lots of practical and they are allowed to use the machines.As a result, they know how to drill, cut and use the machines.Another second-year male Computer Engineering student (2ME9) indicated "I think it also depends on the lecturer teaching the course.Some lecturers are able to interact more with their students as compared with the others.For example, all my mates are complaining about engineering technology course, but my lecturer had more practical sessions with us.It all depends on the lecturer teaching the course."

These observations suggest that the number of practical sessions could vary among departments, lecturers and the stage of the students.It appears a lot more practical are held in the latter years than the early years and this does not meet the expectations of the students as expressed in the previous quotes.
Inadequate orientation for students about the engineering programme and what to expect

It was also revealed that some of the experiences especially in the early years in the university are the result of inadequate orientation of the students about the courses and their expectations.Most of the students indicated that they were made to take some core courses that they did not expect or were not related to engineering.They felt that those courses were irrelevant and contributed to increasing their stress.Some of the students felt the non-engineering courses they were taught in the first and second years were a waste of time but admitted they have now realised their importance as they advance to higher levels of their studies.Here are quotes by two females and one male to illustrate this experience:

"When I was in the first year first semester, it was very stressful; assignments and drawings and when the lecturer sees your drawing, he just looks at it and tells you to re-draw without telling you your errors.They can give you about 6 drawings to do.At that point, I regretted choosing engineering, but I have now adjusted to the system, so I no longer regret it" [second-year female Petroleum Eng. 2FE5]."When I got to school in the first year, I had this mentality that I would be taught more about computers, but it was a lot different; technical drawing and all those things.So, I wasn't enjoying the course in the first year but gradually my interest increased.I realised later that it's not just about computers, but you must know math and other subjects.Although I like math, I struggled because some of my expectations were not met, and it affected my performance" [final year female Computer Eng. 4FE2]."We are all mandated to take a course in introductory sociology, which I think has no link with engineering.Even if we had to take such courses then I think it should be more related to the field of study.I would have expected that the design of that course for engineering students should be different from that for social science students to make it more relevant" [second-year male Biomedical Eng.2ME8]."When I first entered the university, I had this idea that I would be studying medical devices including anatomy and physiology throughout my four years in school.But in one semester, we took courses in French, Economics, and Literature.At that time, I thought they were irrelevant but now I can see that they were not only preparing us for your career but also helping us to enhance our personal skills."[final year female Biomedical Eng.4FE4].

A discussion with the lecturers however revealed that orientations are organised for the students, but some do not take it seriously to fully participate.They also indicated that students' participation could be improved by restructuring it and reconsidering the timing as some fresh students report to school after the orientation period is over.They also agreed that there are currently no standardised teaching methods for engineering programmes hence the lecturers apply different teaching approaches, some of which may not be effective and gender-responsive.
Barriers within the psychosocial or emotional learning environment
Inadequate involvement of females in practical work

The limited laboratory space and equipment coupled with the low number of women studying engineering as well as stereotypes about gender roles have influenced the way female students are treated by their male counterparts and supervisors especially during practical sessions.Female engineering students reported that their male counterparts and some supervisors limit their participation in certain tasks during the practical sessions and these practices reportedly reduce their confidence level and restrict their exploratory abilities.There were, however, mixed feelings about how the girls are treated by the boys.Some quotes are presented below to support these findings.

A third-year female Petroleum Engineering student (3FE7) said that it is a good feeling to have few girls among many boys because the boys are very supportive and most of the time, when the females do not understand certain topics, they approach the males for help, and they gladly help them.For most of the female FGD participants, the support they receive from their male counterparts could come along with some disadvantages as portrayed in the following quotes by three female students: "It's a very nice feeling being the only female among males.But for me, the disadvantages that I faced were that they restrict you from doing some things.They are like, 'you're a lady and what are you coming to do?' They don't even understand why you are doing the engineering so, I told them that no, I came to learn so, why don't they allow me to do what I came here to do?They keep telling me this work is for men.Though they will pamper you, they will not allow you to learn.You must push yourself on them before they will allow you to learn.It's not encouraging; they should be pushing us to learn more" [third year female Biomedical Eng.3FE6]."The surveying aspect of our course is mostly practical.Sometimes we go to the field, and we have only one or two instruments for 131 students.When we the ladies take the instruments to use the men tell us we are slow.They keep telling us they are in a hurry and want to work and go, and we feel bad.They don't have patience for us.They must understand that we are ladies, and they must consider us.The ladies are only 13" [third year female Geomatic Eng.3FE1]."One day, when we had to mix cement during practical session, I tried to do it and one of my male classmates told me as a girl, I shouldn't be mixing cement -it's for men" [second year female Civil Eng.2FE8].

Although the male students were of the view that the engineering girls are very intelligent, they did acknowledge that they tend to be relatively slower compared to the males during practical work.The men were also of the view that some of the tasks that are carried out in the lab could be too strenuous for the women considering their biological makeup.However, the approach they adopt in a bid to help and protect the women could be perceived as intimidating.These views were expressed by three male students in the following statements:

"In my class, ladies are in a way intimidated especially when we go to the lab because I remember when we were dismantling a vehicle engine, you know it's very bulky and ladies cannot go close to raising that heavy machine, so at that point in time they are set aside to just stand and watch.And you know, the guys were doing it; we opened all the bolts and stuff, we opened, removed all the parts then assembled it then we went away.The girls didn't even know how the thing was done.Because mechanical engineering mostly involves the use of muscles especially in the automation labs the girls are set aside, and they watch us do everything [third year male Mechanical Eng.3ME3]."The girls are too emotional, but engineering is not about emotions.Imagine you've been under the sun for 5 hours and you're just a few minutes to end your project and there are girls handling the telescope.If they see a lizard in the bush they'll shout "Ei snake!Snake!" and run away collapsing everything and you'll have to start all over again" [fourth-year male Geomatic Eng.4ME7]."In my class there has never been an instance of a gentleman intimidating a lady, however, if we are doing lab work which involves heavy duty, we set them aside not as a way of intimidating them but just for their safety and we do the work by ourselves.Sometimes, we give them the opportunity to do it, but it turns out that everything becomes slow and time-consuming because something that 2 boys can accomplish in a minute, you will need 10 ladies to accomplish it in an hour.So sometimes it's better to set them aside when we are doing vigorous work" [third year male Civil Eng.3ME6].

Apparently, some of the female students have also experienced some forms of discrimination during their internships outside the school environment.Here are some quotes by female students to support this: My mate and I interned at a hospital and as usual, when the supervisors are going to do field and electronic stuff they just come and call the boys.And we are left behind to do the emailing, faxing, printing.This always puts us on urge because if we are always doing photocopying, excuse me to say I would have gone to a secretarial cafe to learn that -do you get me?And sometimes, we go, and we don't do anything the whole day and the boys are just out of the office doing stuff.Is it that I'm a woman so I can't hold a screwdriver?"[fourth year female Biomedical Eng.4FE4].

While some of these treatments may be seen as discriminatory, some of the students were of the view that they aligned with the Ghanaian cultural values where women are supposed to be protected and handled gently by men.But it is in the interest of the women to choose between cultural values and work.Here are supporting quotes from two fourthyear female students:

"I think we ladies too shouldn't pick and choose.We are asking to be involved in all aspects of engineering work so it's either we're all in or all out.Where I did my internship, they do a lot of bridges and roads.Imagine it is raining, or the machine is spoilt and it's giving off a lot of dust.Due to our culture, the men will give the lady a place to stand so the rain or dust doesn't get into her hair.Culturally, there are some advantages that ladies have over the men, but these are seen to be conflicting with work.You can't pick and choose.It's either you stand in the rain with the men and do the work or you don't" [fourth-year female Civil Eng, 4FE14].In second year, when I did my internship, I was the only girl.One day, it was raining heavily, and the boys were standing in the rain.My supervisor asked, 'young lady, will you want to continue, or you want to go and stand under the shade?'I told him I would like to stand under the shade, however, upon a second thought I just took off my wig cap and joined the boys in the rain and started drilling.In fact, I realised that I got tired, but I proved that I was capable.From that day, whenever they were going to the field, they would come to me and ask, 'we are going to the field, would you want to go' and I would say yes.So, I think as women, we must show that we are ready for the task" [fourth-year female Geomatic Eng.4FE7].
The backlash and apathetic attitude when women become group leaders.

To compensate for their limited involvement in practical sessions, the practical supervisors, who are mostly teaching assistants and technicians, make the female students' leaders of groups that have been formed for practical work.The following quotes by two male students illustrate this: "The lab assistants give the women special treatment like allowing them to use the few chairs in the lab.Because they are few, if a girl misses a class, the lecturer or lab assistant notices so they are active.The ladies are sometimes made group leaders because the lab assistants think the girls can handle the groups very well" [secondyear male Civil Eng.2ME6]."I think they are made group leaders because sometimes there is only one lady in a group and that is the only way to get them involved" [second-year male Mechanical Eng.2ME4].

In some cases, this arrangement does not go down well with the boys as they tend to be apathetic and adopt a 'do it and let's see' attitude while some men think girls alone cannot perform engineering tasks successfully.These were expressed by one female and two male students in the following statements:

"They put us in different groups and each group has a girl.The girl is always the leader of the group.I think it's the norm now.And in my class, if you're a female leader you do most of the lab work.If there's an experiment, the boys will push you to the front and say, 'You are the group leader, go and do it'.Do this, do this, do that.And some of them will help you but others will just sit and watch because all that matters is that your name is written in the attendance sheet.So, a lot of times you are left to do the work, which is a problem for me.Sometimes before you realise you are carrying one engine block by yourself [final year female Mechanical Eng.4FE13]."In Geomatic Engineering, about 30% of our education is on the field so we are divided into sub-groups.I have noticed that when you have more girls than boys, participation is different and when you have less girls than boys it's also a different situation.So based on that I can say that when you have say 2 boys and 10 girls in a group they want the boys to know that they too understand the task and can do it without the boys.So, we need to tread cautiously else a time will come when things get out of hand.I think that men should still dominate the field or else engineering won't be engineering -let's say 40 females:60 males" [fourth-year male Geomatic Eng.4ME7]."Because the ladies are few, I've also realised that we are put in groups, and they normally share the ladies amongst all the groups.I've realised that the ladies don't like to move together with other ladies.So, I asked one lady, and she said 'Oh, it's because of petty problems' and I did not understand.So, they normally feel comfortable when they are with guys than when they are all ladies.So, I feel that all ladies group may not work" [fourth year male Aerospace Eng.4ME9].

Sometimes, the behaviour of the practical session supervisors and technicians further worsens the plights of the female students.But it is also relieving that some of the girls adopt various coping strategies to overcome the 'intimidation' and learn to do things by themselves.This was also observed by the girls during internship as reported earlier by a fourth-year female Geomatic Engineering student (4FE7) who decided to join the men to work while it was raining heavily.In the following statements, a fourth-year female Electrical Engineering student expressed her disappointment about a technician she had expected to guide her perform some tasks in the lab and how his behaviour pushed her to learn:

"We were supposed to solder some wires together.I've never held a solder nor an iron before.The group was large, so I was standing on a chair at the back to try and see what the technician was doing but I didn't get it.So, I was the last person to take the soldering iron to try and put it together, but I couldn't do it.The technician just came, looked at me and called a boy to do it for me.The boy came, did it for me and that was it, we were done with the practical.I didn't learn anything; I didn't really understand how it was being done and nobody really cared.So, in the second year when we had a project involving soldering, I had to get a friend to teach me" [fourth year female Electrical Eng.4FE9].

Another strategy adopted by the girls to ensure their full participation in practical work was to form an all-girls group, though reluctantly.This was illustrated by the following statement by fourth-year female Computer Engineering student: "In our third year, we were supposed to work on a project.We were expected to choose our group members up to 10 students.Only 8 girls are in the class so most of the time the girls only write the reports and don't get involved in the practical work.That is a major issue for me, so I told myself that I don't want to be writing reports, I want to participate.So, I told another lady 'Why don't we form an all-girl group'.

At the beginning, we were wondering whether the boys wouldn't feel like it's this 'women empowerment' thing.But we knew we wanted to do things ourselves.I knew if I joined the mixed sex group the boys would do everything for me if I was willing because they are very good.But I decided that this time, I wanted to do something on my own and all the girls in the class formed the group and worked on that project.It was challenging but we learned through the process.So sometimes if you don't realise that you must do something for yourself, it'll be challenging.The boys will just tell you to sit down and do nothing.They really want to pamper the girls but if you don't plan to do it on your own, you won't learn much.We tried our best and we were able to do it" [Fourth year female Computer Eng. 4FE2].
Silencing and intimidating the female students in class

Apart from the seemingly intimidating actions the women face during practical work, actions by some male lecturers during classes are perceived to be intimidating and could cause the girls to remain silent in class.The females indicated that on the one hand, when they answer questions correctly some male lecturers praise them for doing so.On the other hand, when a girl answers a question wrongly, some lecturers pass intimidating comments.Below are some quotes from two female and two male students to illustrate this:

"Per my interaction with some of my mates, you could realize that most of the females are medicine oriented.One thing I realised is that every female in the class has problems with the Maths and electrical aspects of the Biomedical Engineering.The ladies fall short and come to us for help but when it comes to anatomy, they are good.I think the ladies also lack self-confidence" [second-year male Biomedical Eng.2ME8].There was a time in class a guy said, 'guys, tomorrow everyone should bring his drawing board' and one lady questioned: 'do you mean we are also guys?' So, in a way the ladies feel intimidated, and I see that in my class often.Because mechanical engineering mostly involves the use of muscles especially in the automation labs the women are set aside, and they watch us do everything.By this action, they feel dejected, being oppressed and discriminated against" [third year male Mechanical Eng.3ME3]."One lecturer was always intimidating us.When you stand up to ask a question, he'll be like 'Which high school are you from?No wonder you can't answer this question'.It was so depressing so I called my father one time and told him I wouldn't want to offer the chemical engineering again and my brothers talked to me and encouraged me.In the second semester of first year, it wasn't any better but in second year, I decided to do it because I was determined to compete with the boys and not feel intimidated.Though the pressure is still there, I having been coping and managing to study hard" [fourth year female Chemical Eng.4FE10].That same lecturer used to attack the girls, in particular.We were over hundred in class with only 11 girls.He learned all our names and immediately he asks a difficult question and knows nobody knows the answer, he will call a girl.When you can't answer a question, he would start saying you should have been at home cooking.There was a girl in my class who really suffered during that semester because for almost everything, he'll call her name.She is very good.Sometimes she solved those problems he thought she couldn't solve, and he'll ask us to clap for her but most of the time he'll say: "Why are you wearing big earrings?Remove it.It made me very angry, and I stopped going to his class in the middle of the semester because I could not take it, and the boys will also be gingering him up to go on" [fourth year female Civil Eng.4FE13].

Also, girls who often ask questions in class are labelled by the males as 'too known' and to avoid such labels the girls choose to be silent thus further reducing their inquisitiveness and the quest for knowledge and understanding.According to a third-year female Biomedical Engineering student, some of these comments have reduced the confidence level of the girls and hence they have become timid and unable to even ask questions in class.Her statement is as follows:

"When I came to the first year, I was asking questions in class, but I never saw any female ask questions until we got to second semester when I saw another female ask questions.I thought we were the only two females who had questions to ask.But I was wrong because some girls in the class started approaching me to ask questions on their behalf.At first, I wondered if it was weird for a girl to ask questions but then some of the boys told me they didn't like me because I asked a lot of questions.So, I think females don't feel bold to express themselves because of the notion behind you asking questions.My lecturers answer me and that clears any doubts in my mind but it's the male students who complain about that.I stopped asking questions on behalf of the girls, but I ask only for myself" [third year female Biomedical Eng.3FE6].

It also came to light that though there is no prescribed dress code, the style of dressing by some of the female students gives rise to some comments from the lecturers, which were considered intimidating.Quotes from three four-year female students illustrate this:

"With respect to dressing, I think there is a perception that engineering girls are not supposed to look nice or be fashionable.But I think that is the archaic mentality.I think we are trying to break the odds; times have changed so in as much as we are smart, we are still women, and we can't sacrifice our femininity because we are offering engineering" [fourth year female Civil Eng.4FE14]."I think it's for the lecturers to tell us to dress decently and come to class.But they can't tell us to wear this or that.No, it's not appropriate.If we were in high school, you can say that there's a dress code but in the university there's no dress code.When I went to class for one of my courses, there was a lecturer who was always on me when I braided my hair.He'd ask me "Are you sure you are an engineering student?Can your helmet fit on your hair?Why don't you go and do Real Estates programme?Why don't you go and do Fashion?"He said it in front of the whole class, and everyone was looking at me.How did he expect me to feel?I just had to let go of what he said.Already, engineering is perceived to be for males, and we are coming in to offer engineering and then you make us feel this way, it won't help" [fourth year female Geomatic Eng.4FE8]."I think sometimes, it's not totally the fault of the lecturers when they attach ladies.Because sometimes we ladies think we have the freedom to do such dressing, some lecturers won't allow you to be in their class -they will sack you.There was this lecturer who said he doesn't like ladies who add extensions to their hair.So, no matter how you dress, this lecturer will attack you.I was once a victim.Sometimes even when you dress very formally, your lecturer will see you and say 'you are an engineering student, wear shorts' because the boys wear shorts and trousers to class.I was called once because I wore shorts that were below my knees, and he said why am I wearing three-quarters?I should either wear full trousers or a dress or a skirt, and I was confused because the people I was with were wearing shorts.They even had slides; they were wearing slippers to class, but I was wearing shoes" [fourth year female Geomatic Eng.4FE7].

Despite the intimidating acts presented in the previous section, there are some male and female lecturers who motivate and encourage the students through their actions.Here are some supporting quotes by six female and one male students: "In class when a male answers a question wrongly and then a female answers it correctly, the boys will say you're intelligent.The lecturers also sometimes say the ladies are doing well since we are only a few women with over 100 boys" [second year female Petroleum Eng. 2FE5]."Last semester when we were having one of the programming courses and I was late for one lecture the lecturer said we the ladies should come inside but the guys were still made to stand outside.The guys were murmuring since they were made to stay outside.He said the boys must learn their lesson so that it will make them come to class early and learn to be professionals" [second year female Telecommunication Eng, 2FE2]."For my course, we have only male lecturers in the department, and they are more relaxed towards the girls.They are more accommodating towards the girls when we approach them with problems" [second year female Electrical Engineering 2FE9]."Yes, some lecturers, not all of them, try to help us to be at the top and not get intimidated by the course" [fourth year female Petrochemical Eng.4FE12]."For my department, we've had only male lecturers.They've been good.One of the lecturers will tell you that he met his wife in his class; Discussion and conclusion

This study sought to identify barriers within the learning environment that could influence the retention of women in higher engineering education.Both men and women were involved in the study to help identify barriers that are common to both sexes as well as those peculiar to each sex.This also enabled us to confirm and better understand some of the issues raised by each sex.The main challenges identified have been categorised into barriers within the physical, pedagogical and psychosocial learning environments.The barriers within the physical learning environment relate to (1) inadequate furniture and lecture rooms, and (2) inadequate laboratory space and equipment.Barriers within the pedagogical learning environment include (1) outmoded curriculum and poor teaching methods, (2) inadequate practical sessions, and (3) inadequate orientation for fresh students about the engineering programme and what to expect during their students.Barriers within the psychosocial or emotional learning environment include (1) inadequate involvement of females in practical work, (2) the backlash and apathetic attitudes of males when women become group leaders, (3) silencing and intimidating the female students in class, and (4) limited female role models.

Students' experiences in the physical learning environment such as overcrowded lecture rooms support earlier studies by Closs et al. (2022), Rusticus et al. (2023) and UNESCO (2012) that found that large class sizes hinder interactions, active participation, students' feeling of connectedness and desire to express themselves more freely.Whereas we found that overcrowded lecture rooms distract classroom teaching and learning, Closs et al. (2022) and Chambliss and Takacs (2014) observe that large lecture rooms could also cause distractions as students are spread out and everybody is sitting in isolation and doing their own things on their laptops or phones while the lecturer wanders around and does not interact with the students.The demotivating effects of the barriers in the physical learning environment, such as inadequate laboratory equipment, as well as barriers in the pedagogical learning environment, such as inadequate practical sessions, outmoded curriculum, and poor teaching methods, have also been reported by Godfrey and King (2011).The negative experiences associated with these barriers align with other studies that report that the level of interest among women in science is influenced by their overall learning experience in school (Baker, 2013;UNECSO, 2016), the STEM teachers (Robnett, 2015;Stearns et al., 2016) and their teaching strategies (Baker, 2013;OECD, 2015;Spearman & Watt, 2013), the curriculum (Baker, 2013) and opportunities for practice (Skolnik, 2015).

The findings also support Closs et al. (2022) and Rusticus et al. (2023) who found that their study participants, i.e. Business and Economics students in an Australian University and Psychology students in a Canadian University, respectively, felt more motivated when their lecturers actively engage them in class discussions.They further explained that this knowledge and experience sharing enhance knowledge co-creation and enables students to gain a better understanding of the relevance of what they are learning to their careers.Some of the challenges experienced within the pedagogical learning environment were found to be the result of inadequate orientation of students during their early stages in the university.Some of the displeasure about low levels of practical sessions and taking non-engineering courses would not have arisen if they had been given adequate orientation.Whereas both female and male students faced similar challenges in the physical learning environment, the effects of overcrowded lecture rooms tend to affect males in a way that they are sometimes made to remain outside the lecture rooms as some lecturers give the females the preference to fill in the limited space.In relation to inadequate laboratory space and equipment, both female and male students are affected however, it aggravates the practice of setting aside women during practical sessions.

Most of the challenges engineering women faced within the learning environments are largely due to the psychosocial dimension combined with some aspects of physical and pedagogical learning environments.The inadequate involvement of female students in practical work due to limited laboratory facilities combined with gender stereotypes has been reported by Baker (2000).This author found that lack of laboratory facilities hinders learning but also increases the risk of boys monopolising the material and girls becoming observers.It was also found that there is the backlash and apathetic attitude by men when women become group leaders, and these behaviours can be explained from the expectation states theory (Berger et al., 1974).This theory suggests that gender role expectations cause perceivers to display supportive or more critical behaviour towards a person, depending on whether the person is viewed as having the task-relevant knowledge and abilities.The findings show the influence of gender role expectations on behaviours of individuals, groups and task givers (Hoyt & Murphy, 2016).

The challenge of silencing female students in class due to intimidation was also observed by Sadker et al. (2009) and Heaverlo et al. (2013) in some classrooms where girls have less instructional and discussion time, ask fewer questions, and receive less praise than boys.This practice of intimidating the girls will worsen their experiences if the principles of the theory of feminist pedagogy are ignored.Among others, the theory highlights that acknowledging differences in identities allow for equity-mindedness and a desire for justice and fairness that considers specific identities and needs of students within a specific context, rather than assuming that everyone in the classroom is the same (Bostow et al., 2015).Closs et al. (2022) who conducted their study among Business and Economics students also observed that gender considerations combined with intersectional factors such as ethnicity or race could create a tense atmosphere for girls causing them to remain silent when in class or working with boys in groups.They note that in such situations the girls become 'invisible' to the boys and even teachers.It is also interesting that female students' style of dressing could also be a source of intimidation.This could largely be informed by Ghanaian cultural values as well as the inability of male lecturers to recognise the effects of modernity as well as the different identities they must deal with as the number of females in their classes increase year after year.

The behaviour of some male students and supervisors in the assignment of tasks supports Eagly and Karau (2002) who note that gender role expectation influences allocation of tasks and responsibilities to individuals and groups whereby women will usually be given tasks or be excluded from certain tasks based on the perceived gender roles.Our study revealed that these treatments are not only limited to the school environment but are also perpetuated during students' internships.Closs et al. (2022) reports that despite the benefits offered by group assignments, managing them was one of the most difficult challenges mentioned by teachers they interviewed.This could also explain why the mixed sexes engineering practical groups were not properly supervised and managed to ensure a fair participation and contribution of each member of the group.The kind of instructions given by the technicians to the students align with Keller (2001) who found that teachers can pass on gender stereotypes to their students through instructions.Some studies have found that boys may take leadership roles, argue and defend their views while girls may take stereotypical, secondary and more passive roles, have less opportunity to speak in groups and avoid confrontation with their peers (Leman et al., 2016).

The challenge of limited female role models, where some of the students had never been taught by a female since they entered the University supports Knezek et al. (2015) who highlights the importance of role models and mentorship opportunities in influencing women's interest and retention in STEM.The limited number of female lecturers and supervisors in the university might also have contributed to the experiences reported by the students.There were, however, several quotes from female students suggesting that some female and male lecturers influenced them positively.This finding aligns with Baker (2013) and Stearns et al. (2016) who indicated that female teachers can positively influence girls' education in STEM by dispelling myths about sex-based innate abilities among boys and acting as role models for girls.The female lecturers may also be more sensitive to the needs of girls and have positive attitudes towards gender equality in the classroom than their male counterparts.An example from our study was the indication by some female students that female lecturers and technicians understand them better when they have biologically related issues such as dysmenorrhea, and they feel more comfortable disclosing such issues to female than male lecturers.This study has also shown that while women are aware of gender stereotypes that exclude them from performing some tasks, they realise the importance of getting involved in learning activities so they try to overcome such exclusions by ignoring cultural values, exerting their confidence level, being assertive and working hard.

This exploratory study has shown that once enrolled, both male and female engineering students experience challenges including limited laboratory space and equipment, overcrowded lecture rooms, outmoded curriculum, poor teaching methods, and ineffective public address systems however, the effects are expressed differently by both sexes.A major barrier peculiar to females is intimidation by some male students, technicians and lecturers during theoretical and practical classes, which reduces their confidence level and exploratory abilities.Other female related barriers within the psychosocial learning environment are exclusion of females from performing some tasks and limited female role models to provide mentorship and guidance.
Practical implication

In Ghana, efforts are being made at the national and institutional levels to bridge the gender gap in education and STEM in general.These include the introduction of the Science, Technology and Mathematics Education (STME) Clinic for Girls in 1987 to promote STEM education among girls; the establishment of Girls' Education Unit in 1997 to work towards the reduction of gender disparities in education; and the establishment of the Science Education Unit to introduce programmes aimed at increasing students' enrolment in STEM subjects.At the professional level, the Ghana Institution of Engineering (GhIE), in 1999, established the Women in Engineering (WinE) Unit to, among others, encourage young women to consider engineering as an option for study when entering university.Both the International Day of Women and Girls in Science and World Engineering Day are celebrated in Ghana every year with the participation of pupils and students and other stakeholders to promote STEM and engineering, respectively.In the university that we studied, there is the gender policy with strategies including adoption of concessionary measures in male-dominated disciplines, e.g. by lowering admission cutoff point by 1 for female STEM applicants and ensuring gender equity in the award of scholarships.The university also has the Equality and Diversity Policy that seeks to, among others, increase the proportion of women in senior academic leadership roles.The Teaching and Learning Policy of this university has the goal to enhance teaching and learning activities by providing guidelines to all academic and support staff and students.The Mentorship policy for staff professional development has programmes where older and experienced lecturers mentor newer ones, and there is a mentorship programme for fresh and continuing students.Furthermore, the university organises outreach programmes at high schools and teacher training institutions to introduce them to the various STEM programmes offered in the university.

While these efforts are being made, it is critical to consider other factors that influence students' experiences and subsequently reduce their interest in STEM, especially engineering.The gender stereotypes and societal and cultural issues experienced by the students within the university environment call for sensitisation about engineering and its prospects and how women's participation is possible and crucial.The negative experiences of female engineering students within the university learning environment need to be corrected if we should expect more women in engineering fields.It is high time the management of universities realised that as more females are being enrolled in engineering programmes, the curriculum that was previously heavily masculinised should be adjusted to meet the needs of female students as well.This implies that lecturers, laboratory technicians as well as students (females and males) need to be sensitised and trained on the importance of gender equity and gender mainstreaming in teaching and learning activities in the university.There is also a need for professional development of lecturers especially in pedagogies that are effective and relevant for engineering education.Some recommendations to the management of the university include revising the curriculum to make it more practical and gender-responsive, recruiting and retaining more female lecturers, standardising teaching methods, increasing the number of practical sessions, and reducing student-lecturer ratio by employing more lecturers.The effects of overcrowded lecture rooms may be addressed by exploring and advancing e-learning options and enhancing the quantity and quality of teaching and learning environment through for example, expanding classroom and laboratory infrastructure.
Policy implications

In Ghana, much of the efforts at increasing students' enrolment in STEM is at the basic and secondary education levels.It is critical that much attention is given to the tertiary levels, especially in the public universities, by improving the STEM teaching and learning facilities including lecture rooms, laboratories and equipment for practical lessons.These will help address the challenges of reducing intake of students, overcrowding and limited opportunities for practical lessons, which affect females in various ways as revealed in this study.Ghana currently has a draft STEM education policy with the goal of achieving improved access to STEM education at all levels and improved skills and competencies of STEM teachers in interactive pedagogy founded on best practices.The findings from this study have shown the need for the draft policy to integrate gender-responsive strategies that will not only increase enrolment of girls in engineering and other STEM fields but also address the societal, cultural, stereotypical, pedagogical, psychosocial and other teaching and learning-related barriers identified in this study.
Theoretical implication

Rather than using the most frequently used way of assessing learning environments such as 'What Is Happening In this Class?(WIHIC)' or Science Laboratory Environment Inventory (SLEI) (Aldridge et al., 1999;Fraser, 2023;Fraser et al., 1995), this study used qualitative interview method (focus groups) to help gain a more in-depth understanding of students' experiences rather than perceptions in the classroom and laboratory environments.The study contributes to a better understanding of gender dynamics and students' experiences in engineering learning environment.The study highlights the importance of integrating gender considerations into learning environments that are dominated by one gender.It also emphasises the importance of being aware of cultural differences and learning how to treat students equally and fairly (Skordi & Fraser, 2019), helping to avoid isolation, intimidation and prejudice, and supporting diverse relationships to help improve the quality of students' learning experience (Arkoudis et al., 2019).

The findings have also shown the importance of the application of feminist pedagogy and expectation states theories in understanding the barriers to female participation in engineering learning environments.Specifically, the expectation states theory (Berger et al., 1974) suggests that gender role expectations can cause people to support or victimise a person, depending on the extent to which the person is viewed as having the task-relevant knowledge and abilities.For this reason, male students and technicians exclude females from tasks they perceive not to be in alignment with their gender roles.When the principles of the feminist pedagogy theory (Bostow et al., 2015) is applied in the learning environment, everyone recognises the importance of differences in identities and ensures that there is no discrimination or intimidation based on gender and other intersectional factors as found in our study.
